cemc-fryer-2022-01a.title: Add and subtract
cemc-fryer-2022-01a.body:
4 hits add $7 \times 4 = 28$ points and 2 misses subtract $3 \times 2 = 6$ points, so the score is $28 - 6 = 22$.

**Answer: 22**

cemc-fryer-2022-01b.title: Work backwards
cemc-fryer-2022-01b.body:
The 6 misses cost $18$ points, so the hits earned $59 + 18 = 77$ points. That is $77 \div 7 = 11$ hits.

**Answer: 11**

cemc-fryer-2022-01c.title: Write the score in terms of $m$
cemc-fryer-2022-01c.body:
With $m$ misses there are $20 - m$ hits, so the score is $7(20 - m) - 3m = 140 - 10m$.

We need $85 < 140 - 10m < 105$, i.e. $35 < 10m < 55$, i.e. $3.5 < m < 5.5$. Since $m$ is an integer, $m = 4$ or $m = 5$.

Check: $m = 4$ gives $7 \cdot 16 - 12 = 100$ and $m = 5$ gives $7 \cdot 15 - 15 = 90$.

**Answer: $m = 4$ or $m = 5$**

cemc-fryer-2022-01c.title: Guess and adjust
cemc-fryer-2022-01c.body:
$m = 3$: score $7 \cdot 17 - 9 = 110$, too big. $m = 4$: score $100$ ✓. $m = 5$: score $90$ ✓. $m = 6$: score $98 - 18 = 80$, too small.

Each extra miss lowers the score by 10 (lose a 7 and gain a $-3$), so no other values work.

**Answer: $m = 4$ or $m = 5$**

cemc-fryer-2022-02a.title: Inclusion–exclusion
cemc-fryer-2022-02a.body:
Adding the two rectangles counts the overlap twice, so the area of $ABGH$ is $13 + 13 - 5 = 21\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: $21\text{ cm}^2$**

cemc-fryer-2022-02a.title: Split into pieces
cemc-fryer-2022-02a.body:
$ABFE$ has area $13 - 5 = 8\text{ cm}^2$, and $ABGH$ is $ABFE$ together with $EFGH$: $8 + 13 = 21\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: $21\text{ cm}^2$**

cemc-fryer-2022-02b.title: Areas in thirds
cemc-fryer-2022-02b.body:
Let $|\triangle KLN| = x$. Since it is half of $\triangle JKL$, also $|\triangle JKN| = x$. The triangles are identical, so $|\triangle MLN| = x$ too.

The figure $JKLMN$ consists of $\triangle JKN$, $\triangle KLN$ and $\triangle MLN$, so $3x = 48$ and $x = 16$.

Then $|\triangle JKL| = 2x = 32$. The triangle is right-angled at $K$, so $\tfrac12 (JK)(KL) = 32$, i.e. $\tfrac12 (6)(KL) = 32$, giving $KL = \tfrac{32}{3}$ cm.

**Answer: $KL = \frac{32}{3}$ cm**

cemc-fryer-2022-02c.title: Find the small triangle first
cemc-fryer-2022-02c.body:
The figure $PQTUS$ is the rectangle $PQRS$ plus $\triangle URT$, so $|\triangle URT| = 117 - 108 = 9\text{ cm}^2$.

The triangle $PQT$ is $PQRU$ plus $\triangle URT$, so $|PQRU| = 81 - 9 = 72\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: $72\text{ cm}^2$**

cemc-fryer-2022-03a.title: Prime factorize
cemc-fryer-2022-03a.body:
$675 = 3^3 \times 5^2$. A factor has 0–3 threes (4 choices) and 0–2 fives (3 choices), so there are $4 \times 3 = 12$ factors.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-fryer-2022-03b.title: Smallest required number
cemc-fryer-2022-03b.body:
$n$ has $4 + 14 = 18$ factors. Since $9 = 3^2$, $11$, $15 = 3 \cdot 5$ and $25 = 5^2$ divide $n$, $n$ is divisible by $3^2 \times 5^2 \times 11$.

$3^2 \times 5^2 \times 11$ has $3 \times 3 \times 2 = 18$ factors already. Any extra prime factor (or larger exponent) would give more than 18 factors, so $n = 3^2 \times 5^2 \times 11 = 2475$.

**Answer: $n = 2475$**

cemc-fryer-2022-03c.title: Case on the number of prime factors
cemc-fryer-2022-03c.body:
Such an $m$ has 12 factors and is divisible by $2 \times 3^2 = 18$.

**Two primes:** $m = 2^a 3^b$ with $a \ge 1$, $b \ge 2$ and $(a+1)(b+1) = 12$. The options are $(a, b) = (1, 5), (2, 3), (3, 2)$, giving $486, 108, 72$, all less than 500: **3** numbers.

**Three primes:** $m = 2^a 3^b p^c$ with prime $p > 3$. The minimum exponents $(1, 2, 1)$ already give $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 12$ factors, so $m = 18p$. We need $18p < 500$, so $p \le 27$: $p = 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23$, giving **7** numbers.

**Four or more primes:** at least $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 24$ factors, too many.

Total: $3 + 7 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

cemc-fryer-2022-04a.title: Add up the removals
cemc-fryer-2022-04a.body:
All beans come from the 40-bean jar. Franco's 5 turns remove $1 + 3 + 4 + 1 + 3 = 12$ and Sarah's 5 turns remove $2 + 5 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 16$. Since $28 < 40$, every turn could be taken, leaving $40 - 28 = 12$ beans.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-fryer-2022-04b.title: Use the 12-turn cycle
cemc-fryer-2022-04b.body:
Franco's cycle has length 3 and Sarah's has length 2, so after every 12 turns (6 each) both restart. In 12 turns Franco removes $2(1+3+4) = 16$ and Sarah removes $3(2+5) = 21$: 37 beans in total.

After $10 \times 12 = 120$ turns, $384 - 370 = 14$ beans remain and it is Franco's turn at the start of his cycle.

Turn 121: Franco takes 1 (13 left). Turn 122: Sarah takes 2 (11 left). Turn 123: Franco takes 3 (8 left). Turn 124: Sarah takes 5 (3 left). Franco now needs 4 beans and cannot move, so Sarah wins after exactly $n = 124$ turns.

**Answer: $n = 124$**

cemc-fryer-2022-04c.title: Reduce to the last 5 beans
cemc-fryer-2022-04c.body:
Write $T_k$ for turn $k$. There are 23 beans. After $T_4$, $1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 11$ beans are gone, leaving 12. Then some jar has at least 6 beans, so $T_5$ (Franco, 4) is possible, leaving 8; some jar then has at least 4, so $T_6$ (Sarah, 2) and $T_7$ (Franco, 1) are possible, leaving exactly 5 beans.

On $T_8$ Sarah must take 5. She wins if the 5 beans are all in one jar, and loses if they are split $(4, 1)$ or $(3, 2)$. So Franco wins if he can make sure the final 5 beans are not all in one jar.

**Franco's strategy:**
- $T_1$: take 1 bean from the 17-bean jar, giving $(16, 6)$.
- $T_3$: take 3 beans from the jar with fewer beans.
- $T_5$ and $T_7$: take beans from the jar with more beans.

After $T_2$ the jars are $(14, 6)$ or $(16, 4)$, so after $T_3$ they are $(14, 3)$ or $(16, 1)$.

From $T_4$ to $T_7$ only $5 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 12$ beans are removed, so the big jar (14 or 16) cannot be emptied. Franco never touches the small jar again, and Sarah only removes 2 or 5 at a time, so she cannot remove exactly 3 or exactly 1 from it. So the small jar is never emptied either.

After $T_7$ the jars hold $(2, 3)$ or $(4, 1)$, and Sarah cannot remove 5 beans on $T_8$. Franco wins.

**Answer: Franco has a winning strategy.**

cemc-fryer-2022-04d.title: Force the final 12 beans
cemc-fryer-2022-04d.body:
There are 4045 beans. Every 12 turns remove 37 beans (part (b)). After $109 \times 12 = 1308$ turns, $4045 - 109 \cdot 37 = 12$ beans remain, and it is Franco's turn at the start of both cycles. With 12 beans left some jar still has at least 6 beans, so all of the first 1308 turns could be taken.

**Endgames Sarah wins.**
- Final split $(12, 0)$: the moves 1, 2, 3, 5 leave 1 bean, and Franco cannot take 4.
- Final split $(11, 1)$: if Franco takes his 1 from the single bean we are in the $(11, 0)$ case, which Sarah wins the same way. Otherwise the split is $(10, 1)$; the next three moves 2, 3, 5 must all come from the 10-bean jar, leaving $(0, 1)$, and Franco cannot take 4.

**Sarah's strategy.** Choose one jar as the *target* jar.
- While the target jar has 5 or more beans, Sarah always takes from it.
- When it has 2, 3 or 4 beans, she takes her 2s from it and her 5s from the other jar.
- Once it has 0 or 1 bean, she takes from the other jar.

In the first 1308 turns Sarah removes $109 \times 21 = 2289 > 2023$ beans, so she can always bring the target jar down to 0 or 1 bean. (Franco removing beans from the target jar only helps.) Then the other jar holds the remaining 12 or 11 beans, so Sarah can always make her required moves. The final 12 beans are therefore $(12, 0)$ or $(11, 1)$, and Sarah wins.

**Answer: Sarah has a winning strategy.**
